title: "Influential ChatGPT-in-Education Meta-Analysis Retracted: Where's the Transparency and Cost?"
description: "A widely cited meta-analysis claiming ChatGPT improves student learning was retracted by Springer Nature in a two-sentence note plus a non-responsive-author disclosure, after racking up 504 citations and ~500K reads in the year between publication and retraction. Where's the transparency and the cost?"

![Image from [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/05/influential-study-touting-chatgpt-in-education-retracted-over-red-flags/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

> **Retracted paper:** Jin Wang and [Wenxiang Fan](https://orcid.org/0009-0002-7681-0635) (2025), "[The effect of ChatGPT on students' learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-025-04787-y)," *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*, Hangzhou Normal University. [Retracted](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-026-07310-z) April 22, 2026.

[Jeremy Hsu](https://arstechnica.com/author/jeremyhsu/), [reporting](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/05/influential-study-touting-chatgpt-in-education-retracted-over-red-flags/) for *Ars Technica*, walks through the retraction of the [Wang and Fan paper](https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-025-04787-y), a meta-analysis in [*Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*](https://www.nature.com/palcomms/) (Springer Nature) claiming ChatGPT delivers "a large positive impact on improving learning performance," a "moderately positive impact on enhancing learning perception," and gains in "fostering higher-order thinking." The paper pooled effect sizes from 51 prior studies that compared ChatGPT-using experimental groups against non-AI control groups. Springer Nature [retracted it](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-026-07310-z) on April 22, 2026:

> The Editor has decided to retract this paper owing to concerns regarding discrepancies in the meta-analysis. These issues ultimately undermine the confidence the Editor can place in the validity of the analysis and resulting conclusions.
>
> **The authors have not responded to correspondence regarding this retraction.**

What the article reports:

- Between publication on May 6, 2025 and retraction nearly a year later, the paper picked up 262 within-publisher citations, 504 total citations, ~500K reads, and a 99th-percentile attention score.
- [Ilkka Tuomi](https://meaningprocessing.com/), chief scientist at Meaning Processing Ltd., posted on LinkedIn at the time of original publication that meta-analyses of this kind try to "draw conclusions about incompatible and ill-defined outcomes": "The only reason to do these studies seems to be that statistics and meta-analysis tools can crunch out numbers that look [like] science."
- [Ben Williamson](https://www.ed.ac.uk/profile/ben-williamson), senior lecturer at the Centre for Research in Digital Education and the Edinburgh Futures Institute at the University of Edinburgh, told Ars the paper appeared to be "synthesizing very poor quality studies, or mixing together findings from studies that simply cannot be accurately compared due to very different methods, populations, and samples." He also flagged the timing: ChatGPT shipped only two and a half years before publication, and Williamson said it was "not feasible that dozens of high-quality studies about ChatGPT and learning performance could have been conducted, reviewed, and published in that time."
- The retraction notice attracted little attention until Williamson shared it on Bluesky and LinkedIn, raising the worry that the "headline finding that ChatGPT helps learning performance might persist despite its retraction."

The retracted paper's abstract:

> As a new type of artificial intelligence, ChatGPT is becoming widely used in learning. However, academic consensus regarding its efficacy remains elusive. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of ChatGPT in improving students' learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking through a meta-analysis of 51 research studies published between November 2022 and February 2025. The results indicate that ChatGPT has a large positive impact on improving learning performance ($g = 0.867$) and a moderately positive impact on enhancing learning perception ($g = 0.456$) and fostering higher-order thinking ($g = 0.457$). The impact of ChatGPT on learning performance was moderated by type of course ($Q_B = 64.249$, $P < 0.001$), learning model ($Q_B = 76.220$, $P < 0.001$), and duration ($Q_B = 55.998$, $P < 0.001$); its effect on learning perception was moderated by duration ($Q_B = 19.839$, $P < 0.001$); and its influence on the development of higher-order thinking was moderated by type of course ($Q_B = 7.811$, $P < 0.05$) and the role played by ChatGPT ($Q_B = 4.872$, $P < 0.05$). This study suggests that: (1) appropriate learning scaffolds or educational frameworks (e.g., Bloom's taxonomy) should be provided when using ChatGPT to develop students' higher-order thinking; (2) **the broad use of ChatGPT at various grade levels and in different types of courses should be encouraged to support diverse learning needs**; (3) **ChatGPT should be actively integrated into different learning modes to enhance student learning, especially in problem-based learning**; (4) **continuous use of ChatGPT should be ensured to support student learning, with a recommended duration of 4–8 weeks for more stable effects**; (5) **ChatGPT should be flexibly integrated into teaching as an intelligent tutor, learning partner, and educational tool**. Finally, due to the limited sample size for learning perception and higher-order thinking, and the moderately positive effect, future studies with expanded scope should further explore how to use ChatGPT more effectively to cultivate students' learning perception and higher-order thinking.

## My Notes

- **The technical case against the paper has been specific and public from the start.** Tuomi's [methodological analysis](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/what-went-methodologically-wrong-chatgpt-education-ilkka-tuomi-den0f/) and [companion post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ilkka-tuomi-30086_the-effect-of-chatgpt-on-students-learning-activity-7327264463550595073-gl_J/), both posted shortly after the paper appeared, lay it out; Williamson amplified them in [his own pre-publication LinkedIn warning](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ben-williamson-7a501b329_the-effect-of-chatgpt-on-students-learning-activity-7327070885587120128-zRXr/) the same week, telling readers to "check out the two-part analysis by Ilkka Tuomi" before taking the meta-analysis seriously:

  - The paper "repeats all the errors from an earlier meta-analysis by Deng et al.," reusing Deng's search string without attribution, including a copied spelling error.
  - Deng at least tried to score input studies for quality. Wang & Fan say nothing about quality and do not state whether the analyzed studies were peer-reviewed; studies from "0-quality journals (like 'Mathematics' from MDPI)" are included.
  - Internal validity in randomized and quasi-experimental designs requires control and treatment groups drawn from the same population. The 51 studies pool teachers, medical-practice students, college mathematics, computer programming, and language-learning groups; the "basic criterion for making (internally) valid conclusions is broken before the analysis starts."
  - The funnel: the search strings returned 6,621 papers; abstract filtering left 2,712; "careful review" produced 51. In half the studies the experimental/treatment group had fewer than 35 students; some "claim to make statistically valid conclusions based on groups with 12 students," and the paper offers no study-power estimate.
  - The heterogeneity statistic is reported but not interpreted: "huge, suggesting that there is no 'it' in the studies. The external validity is junk."
  - To illustrate what summing effect sizes across incompatible studies looks like, Tuomi compares it to a meta-review of "the impact of electricity on learning outcomes" that would pool teacher commute mode, classroom lighting, and air conditioning into a single average. He calls the pattern "garbage in, gold out": junk inputs, respected-journal output.

- **Publishers should publish a real account of what went wrong, especially for a paper this widely cited.** Two sentences and a non-responsive-author disclosure is not enough from a Springer Nature title that just retracted a paper with 504 citations and ~500K reads, especially when the technical critique above had been public the entire year. The notice does not say which of the three headline claims are now invalid, what the meta-analysis discrepancies actually were, or whether the failure was in study selection, effect-size aggregation, or both. The [Committee on Publication Ethics retraction guidelines](https://publicationethics.org/retraction-guidelines) call for specifics; this notice does not meet that standard. The publisher should also disclose what peer review missed and notify the 262 within-publisher citing authors directly, so the correction reaches them instead of the other way around. Williamson, [writing on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ben-williamson-7a501b329_retraction-note-the-effect-of-chatgpt-on-activity-7456842986551803904-DBoN/) after the retraction, put it bluntly: the paper "should not have been published in the first place," and despite the retraction, "this and similar studies have shaped debates about AI in education anyway."

- **Make get-famous-quick costly for researchers and their institutions.** Publishing fast on a hot topic compounds in upside, while the downside, if it ever arrives, is a thin retraction note years later that does not erase the citations or the attention score. The Wang & Fan paper accumulated nearly 60K accesses and a 200+ altmetric score within three days of publication, per [Williamson's update on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ben-williamson-7a501b329_the-effect-of-chatgpt-on-students-learning-activity-7327070885587120128-zRXr/); by retraction it had reached ~500K reads and 504 citations. Williamson described the broader environment as a "flaky evidentiary culture" in AI-in-education research, "where it's relatively easy to publish in journals with low-quality peer review and editorial processes, allowing papers of dubious quality to get trawled in a poorly designed meta-analysis and then bundled up as conclusive evidence that gets wildly circulated by big social media accounts." A few changes would make the asymmetry hurt:

  - Institutional misconduct review by the authors' employer (Hangzhou Normal University in this case), with a published outcome rather than internal-only handling.
  - Mandatory reciprocal-citation: any paper citing a retracted work after the retraction date must cite the retraction note alongside it, enforced by the publisher inside the same journal family.
  - A publicly searchable retraction registry that travels with the author byline at hiring, grant review, and tenure time. The [Retraction Watch Database](https://retractionwatch.com/retraction-watch-database-user-guide/) already exists; funders and search committees should treat it as a default lookup; few currently do.
  - A grant-cycle penalty: principal investigators with retracted papers in the prior N years carry a disclosure on every new application, weighted in review.

  As long as retraction costs this little, fast publication on a hot topic with weak data has no real downside for the authors or their institutions. The downside lands elsewhere. Papers like Wang & Fan helped legitimize the AI-in-education investment thesis that is [now collapsing](/posts/20260424-edu-startups-decline/), and the schools, districts, and ed-tech vendors that bought in carry the cost. The citation residue stays in the literature long after the funding has moved on.
